packs.title: Gliders, evidence and garden paths
packs.promise: Read glider and windmill stories, collect science evidence and make from an open prairie view.

q.s: Draw an explanation from actual sediment evidence.
st: Find the Sand and Sediments interpretation and choose two readable records linking a sediment layer or profile detail with evidence of an earlier environment.
Note what each record actually says, then describe one difference between the two kinds of evidence. Keep an uncertain reading as a question.

Make a small original diagram in words or pencil: two evidence boxes leading to one tentative landscape explanation. Use your own shapes and wording rather than tracing the exhibit or copying a published diagram.
Add a third box containing a question the evidence does not settle. Mark the supported information and your tentative explanation separately.

q.s: Connect specimens with the evidence beside them.
st: Choose three different currently readable natural-history specimen or habitat records in the opened galleries. Keep your collection in notes, leaving every object in place.
For each record, write its displayed identity and one visible specimen or setting detail you can actually distinguish.
Add one interpretation fact linking that detail to a time, habitat, adaptation or kind of evidence. Label any unsupported connection as a question.
Arrange the three records in a discovery order and give the order a one-line reason. You are organizing evidence, not claiming a new scientific classification.

q.s: Keep a crop, a problem and a response together.
st: Choose three different readable crop or agricultural-technology displays in Hurst Family Exhibit Hall. Record their actual labels or identifying subjects.
For each, note the crop, material or farm task it addresses and one problem stated in its interpretation. Do not supply a problem the source does not mention.
Add the displayed tool, process or technology response and one visible feature connecting it with that task. Keep all objects in place.
Arrange your three records from one farm task to another. Add a question about a trade-off or limitation that your notes do not answer.

packs.title: Depot and Cultural District afternoons
packs.promise: Connect actual music records, public facades, books and galleries across two afternoons.

q.s: Keep actual Walk of Fame records in a small index.
st: Find three different currently readable inductee plaques from a permitted public plaza path. Record each actual name.
For each plaque, note its stated arts role, field or achievement. If the plaque does not state one, use the linked Civic Lubbock account for a supported identification and record that source.
Add an induction date or other displayed date only when it is actually given. Mark missing information as a question rather than filling it from a guess.
Arrange the three names as a small index with one line explaining how their work differs. Keep the records separate from the nearby statue.

q.s: Make an original poster from theater shapes.
st: Choose a permitted sidewalk view and record two actual facade relationships: brick and tile, marquee and wall, opening and edge or another visible pair.
Reduce each observation to an original shape, line or short descriptive word. Do not trace a sign, copy a logo or reuse advertised show wording.
Make a small poster for an imagined, unnamed performance using your own arrangement of those shapes or words. Keep it distinct from the theater’s actual programming.
Revise one part of your poster’s rhythm or balance, then note which real facade detail prompted the change. Give the poster your own title.

q.s: Link actual books through their published records.
st: Choose three different physical books you may inspect in the opened public collection. Handle them according to library directions.
Record each actual title, named author or editor and one publication detail printed in that book, such as publisher, year or edition. Do not copy a passage.
Find a metadata bridge from the first record to the second and another from the second to the third: a shared subject stated by the book, a publication period, editor or another actual connection.
Write your three records and two bridges as a small chain. Add one sentence describing where the chain changes direction. Leave every book in the library’s instructed place.
